prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BOGOTA, Colombia (CNN)  -- Colombian officials are blaming the FARC guerrilla group for a car bombing late Sunday at a police station in Cali that killed two people and wounded at least 14. Residents check out a destroyed police building after a car bombing Sunday night in Cali, Colombia. It was the second bombing in Colombia attributed to the Marxist guerrilla group in less than a week. An explosion at a Blockbuster video rental store in an upscale Bogota neighborhood Tuesday killed two and wounded more than 20. The suspect in Sunday night's attack was killed in a shootout with police after the explosion, Cali Mayor Jorge Ivan Ospina said Monday, hours after convening a special security meeting in the middle of the night. "Although the explosive device only had moderate impact," Ospina said on the Cali government Web site, "we should not forget we are at war and the FARC has been committing terrorist acts in Bogota, Neiva, Cali and other cities in the country. That's why we cannot let our guard down, since they take advantage of Sundays and city centers, where control is more difficult." The explosion came just hours after the rebel group released four hostages in what many interpreted as a gesture to reach a peace accord with the government. Two officials also are slated to be released this week. FARC, which is the Spanish acronym for Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, is the largest and oldest revolutionary group in the nation and has been at war with the government for more than 40 years. According to Ospina, a blue and red Renault 12 Break pickup crashed into the police headquarters in Cali at 10:38 p.m. and then exploded. The driver tried to flee but was felled by two shots from uniformed police and died a few hours later at a hospital, the mayor said. The explosion caused damage in a two-block area, the Cali news Web site Semana.com said. Five of the 14 wounded were minors, Ospina said, citing emergency director Laureano Quintero. The injured are suffering from fractures and other wounds not considered life-threatening, he said. Cali's health minister, Alejandro Varela, said earlier 32 were wounded, including a pregnant woman who was in good condition. Others complained of hearing problems. The mayor's office said the previous higher tally could be a result of people not wounded in the bombing but seeking medical attention to receive government help. Three police were wounded, including a major with a broken arm and an officer who had to have three fingers amputated on his left hand, said the police chief, Gustavo Adolfo Ricaurte Tapia. The bombing caused a temporary power outage, which made security more difficult for officials, said the news Web site Burladero.com. It was the fourth bombing in Cali in less than 42 months, Semana.com said. The latest bombing took place about five blocks from the Palace of Justice, which was blasted by a car bomb in August, killing four and wounding 26. Police buildings were bombed in April 2007 and August 2006. The earlier blast killed five and wounded 17, Semana.com said. Security analysts say FARC has about 9,000 to 12,000 armed guerillas and several thousand supporters, mostly in rural areas. The guerrilla group was established in 1964 as the military wing of the Colombian Communist Party. The guerrillas operate mostly in Colombia but have carried out extortion, kidnappings and other activities in Venezuela, Panama and Ecuador, according to the Federation of American Scientists Intelligence Resource Program. Authorities said Sunday night's bomb contained 90 kilograms (198 pounds) of ammonium nitrate fertilizer and fuel, a commonly used explosive, Semana.com said. By comparison, the bomb that Timothy McVeigh used in the 1995 bombing in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, contained more than 2,800 kilos (6,200 pounds) of ammonium nitrate and diesel fuel.

**BOGOTA, Colombia (CNN) —** Colombian authorities have accused the FARC rebel movement of carrying out a car-bomb attack on a Cali police station late Sunday that left two people dead and at least 14 injured.

Residents later surveyed the wreckage of the police building. The blast was the second attack in less than a week that Colombian officials attributed to the Marxist guerrilla organization. The previous Tuesday, an explosion at a Blockbuster video-rental outlet in an affluent district of Bogota killed two people and injured more than 20.

Cali Mayor Jorge Ivan Ospina said Monday that the suspected perpetrator of Sunday’s bombing was shot by police while trying to escape and died several hours later in a hospital. Ospina made the announcement after calling an emergency security meeting during the night.

In a statement published on Cali’s official website, the mayor said that although the bomb’s force was relatively limited, Colombians must remember that the country remains at war. He accused the FARC of conducting terrorist attacks in Bogota, Neiva, Cali and other Colombian cities. Ospina warned that security forces must remain vigilant because attackers exploit Sundays and crowded urban centers, where maintaining control is more challenging.

The bombing occurred only hours after the rebel group freed four hostages, an action widely seen as an attempt to signal interest in a peace agreement with the government. Two government officials were also expected to be released later that week.

FARC is the Spanish abbreviation for the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia. Founded in 1964 as the armed branch of the Colombian Communist Party, it is Colombia’s oldest and largest revolutionary organization and has fought the government for more than four decades.

According to Ospina, a blue-and-red Renault 12 Break pickup truck struck the Cali police headquarters at 10:38 p.m. before exploding. The driver attempted to run away, but uniformed officers shot him twice. He later died at a hospital.

The Cali news website Semana.com reported that the blast damaged an area spanning two blocks. Ospina, citing emergency-services director Laureano Quintero, said five of the 14 injured people were minors. Those hurt suffered fractures and other injuries, but none were believed to be life-threatening.

Cali Health Minister Alejandro Varela had initially reported 32 injuries, including those of a pregnant woman who was in good condition. Some people also reported hearing difficulties. The mayor’s office said the earlier, higher figure may have included individuals who were not actually injured in the explosion but sought medical care in hopes of qualifying for government assistance.

Police Chief Gustavo Adolfo Ricaurte Tapia said three officers were wounded. Among them were a major who broke an arm and another officer whose injuries required the amputation of three fingers on his left hand.

The explosion briefly knocked out electricity, making it harder for authorities to secure the area, according to the news site Burladero.com.

Semana.com said the incident was Cali’s fourth bombing in fewer than 42 months. It happened roughly five blocks from the Palace of Justice, where an August car bombing killed four people and wounded 26. Police facilities were also bombed in April 2007 and August 2006. The earlier of those two attacks left five dead and 17 injured, the website reported.

Security experts estimate that FARC has between 9,000 and 12,000 armed fighters, as well as several thousand supporters, most of them based in rural regions. Although the group operates primarily within Colombia, it has also engaged in extortion, abductions and other activities in Venezuela, Panama and Ecuador, according to the Federation of American Scientists’ Intelligence Resource Program.

Authorities said the device used Sunday night contained 90 kilograms, or 198 pounds, of ammonium nitrate fertilizer mixed with fuel, a frequently used explosive combination, Semana.com reported. In comparison, the bomb Timothy McVeigh used in the 1995 Oklahoma City attack contained more than 2,800 kilograms, or 6,200 pounds, of ammonium nitrate and diesel fuel.

counterfactuals.prompt: What happened in the late-Sunday car bombing in Cali, and why did Colombian officials blame the FARC? Include casualty figures, official statements, and background on the guerrilla group.
counterfactuals.output:
Late on Sunday, August 31, 2008, a vehicle packed with explosives blew up outside Cali’s Palace of Justice, heavily damaging the courthouse and nearby hotels, shops and homes. Contemporary reports put the toll at **four dead and about 26 wounded**, though the earliest counts varied slightly. Police said the vehicle contained roughly **80 kilograms (175 pounds) of explosives**.

Colombian officials quickly attributed the attack to the **Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, or FARC**. National police chief Gen. Óscar Naranjo said the bomb’s construction and method of attack bore the guerrillas’ hallmarks and that intelligence pointed to a FARC urban unit. Defense Minister Juan Manuel Santos described the bombing as an effort by the rebels to prove they could still strike after suffering major military and political setbacks. President Álvaro Uribe condemned it as a terrorist attack, while authorities offered a reward for information leading to those responsible.

The target also supported the government’s theory: the Palace of Justice housed judges and prosecutors involved in cases against guerrillas and other armed groups. Officials portrayed the bombing as retaliation and an attempt to intimidate the judiciary.

The **FARC**, founded in 1964, was Colombia’s largest and oldest Marxist guerrilla organization. It said it was fighting for rural and social reform but financed much of its insurgency through kidnapping, extortion and involvement in the cocaine trade. By 2008 it had been weakened by a sustained government offensive, the deaths of senior commanders—including founder Manuel “Sureshot” Marulanda and Raúl Reyes—and the rescue of former presidential candidate Ingrid Betancourt and 14 other hostages. Officials therefore viewed the Cali bombing as both a deadly attack and a bid by the diminished group to demonstrate that it remained operational.

**Bomb outside Cali police station kills suspected attacker, wounds dozens**

**CALI, Colombia** — A bomb exploded outside a police station in the southwestern Colombian city of Cali, killing the man authorities believe was transporting the device and injuring numerous police officers and civilians, officials said.

The blast occurred near a police facility in a residential area of Cali, Colombia’s third-largest city. It damaged nearby buildings, shattered windows and sent debris across surrounding streets as emergency crews evacuated the wounded and police sealed off the neighborhood.

Authorities said the only person killed was the suspected bomber, who apparently died when the explosive detonated prematurely. Investigators were examining whether he intended to leave the device near the station or carry out a suicide attack.

Early reports offered conflicting accounts of the number of wounded. Police officials said at least 16 people were injured, while hospital and emergency-service estimates put the total closer to 30. The discrepancy appeared to result from patients being taken to several medical facilities and from some people seeking treatment on their own for cuts, hearing damage and shock.

Most of the injuries were not believed to be life-threatening, officials said.

No group immediately claimed responsibility. Colombian authorities said the attack bore signs of operations previously attributed to the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, or FARC, but cautioned that the investigation was continuing.

### A history of urban attacks

Cali, an important commercial center in the country’s southwest, has long been vulnerable to violence linked to guerrilla organizations, drug-trafficking groups and criminal networks. Its location also makes it strategically significant because routes through the surrounding region connect Colombia’s interior with the Pacific coast.

Colombia has suffered repeated bombings during decades of internal conflict. Among the most notorious was the 2003 bombing of Bogotá’s El Nogal social club, which killed 36 people and wounded more than 150. Colombian authorities blamed the FARC, although the organization denied responsibility.

A 2006 car bombing at a military university in Bogotá wounded more than 20 people. Police stations, army posts, government buildings and local political offices have also been attacked in smaller cities and rural areas.

Security officials said the Cali bombing demonstrated that insurgent and criminal organizations retained the ability to strike in urban centers even after years of military pressure weakened their rural forces.

### Hostage releases brought cautious optimism

The attack came after a series of highly publicized hostage releases had raised hopes that Colombia’s long-running conflict might be entering a less violent phase.

With Venezuelan mediation, the FARC released former vice presidential candidate Clara Rojas and former lawmaker Consuelo González de Perdomo in January 2008. The rebels freed four more former members of Congress the following month.

Those releases were welcomed internationally but left hundreds of captives believed to remain in guerrilla hands. At the time, the FARC continued to hold prominent hostages, including former presidential candidate Ingrid Betancourt, three U.S. defense contractors and members of Colombia’s security forces.

The Colombian government insisted that humanitarian releases should be unconditional. The FARC sought a prisoner exchange and demanded that the government temporarily demilitarize an area where negotiations could take place.

### FARC’s origins and evolution

The FARC was founded in 1964 after the Colombian military attacked a rural enclave controlled by communist-aligned peasants. Emerging from an era of partisan bloodshed known as *La Violencia*, the group presented itself as a Marxist-Leninist movement fighting for land redistribution and political change.

Over the following decades, it grew into Colombia’s largest guerrilla organization, operating across broad areas of the countryside. At its height, the FARC fielded an estimated 15,000 to 20,000 fighters.

The organization financed its insurgency through kidnapping, extortion, illegal mining and taxes imposed on the cocaine trade. The United States, Colombia and the European Union designated it a terrorist organization.

Beginning in the early 2000s, U.S.-backed Colombian military operations drove the rebels from many of their strongholds and killed or captured senior commanders. The FARC nevertheless retained the capacity to plant bombs, ambush security forces and carry out kidnappings.

Authorities in Cali said forensic teams were analyzing the explosive device, surveillance footage and evidence recovered near the dead suspect. Police also increased security around government buildings and other potential targets as investigators searched for accomplices.
